issues.legal_issue: The required publication and local notice for a proposed land acquisition must be contemporaneous, but need not be simultaneous, and a time gap does not by itself invalidate the acquisition.
material_facts: A notification and declaration for a public-purpose land acquisition were published in the official gazette.
Public notice of the substance of the notification was given in the locality 29 days after gazette publication.
The challenge asserted that the interval made the notification invalid.
issues.conclusion: Both steps are required before further action, but they need not occur at the same time or immediately one after the other. They must be contemporaneous; a gap that breaks continuity and raises a prima facie concern about bona fides may require further inquiry into its cause and any resulting prejudice. The interval alleged here did not make the notification invalid merely by itself.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires both gazette publication and public notice in the locality; section 4(2) action cannot precede their completion. Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan and Narinderjit Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh establish that both steps are mandatory. State of Mysore v. Abdul Rajak does not establish that every interval is fatal. The Court approved Sanjivaiah Nagar Depressed and Backward Classes Sangh v. District Collector, Hyderabad and the Full Bench decision in Shahnaz Salima v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, and disapproved Satish Kapur v. State of Haryana, Rattan Singh v. State, C. Suryanarayana v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, and Mohammad Khawaza v. Government of Andhra Pradesh.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.gazette_publication_and_local_notice_bot: The government published the acquisition notification in the official gazette and gave notice of its substance in the locality.
predicates.notice_gap_did_not_break_continuity: The interval between publication and local notice was not shown to be so large that it broke the continuity of the acquisition process.

issues.definition: When both publicity steps occur in a land acquisition proceeding and their interval does not break continuity, the publicity requirements are satisfied despite the steps not being simultaneous.

issues.legal_issue: The period for objecting to a proposed land acquisition begins when both prescribed forms of notice have been completed, measured from whichever was completed later.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette, and notice of its substance was later given in the locality.
The challenge argued that a delay between those steps could curtail the opportunity to object.
issues.conclusion: The objection period runs from the later of gazette publication and local notice, because the notification is issued for this purpose only when the two-step process of notifying the interested public is complete.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides an opportunity for interested persons to object within 30 days after the issue of the notification. Read with section 4(1), “issue” means completion of both gazette publication and local notice. The Court construed the provisions to preserve a reasonable opportunity to object and relied on the mandatory two-step notice process explained in Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan and related decisions.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.gazette_publication_and_local_notice_bot: The government published the acquisition notification in the official gazette and gave notice of its substance in the locality.

issues.definition: When both notice steps occur in a land acquisition proceeding, the objection period begins on the later of those steps.

issues.legal_issue: Pre-notification delay alone does not invalidate the use of urgency powers to dispense with an inquiry into objections to a proposed land acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition was challenged on the ground that the matter had been under interdepartmental correspondence for nearly eight years before the notification and declaration were published.
The challenge argued that this delay showed that there was no urgency to dispense with the objections inquiry.
issues.conclusion: The length of time spent before publication does not, by itself, render invocation of the urgency provisions invalid; delay may even make the need for acquisition more urgent.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(4) and 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 concern dispensing with the objections inquiry when urgency provisions are invoked. Jaga Ram v. State of Haryana holds that earlier governmental lethargy is not decisive of whether urgency existed when the notification was issued. Kashi Reddy Papaiah v. Government of Andhra Pradesh holds that officials’ delay in taking earlier steps does not nullify urgency existing at the time of notification.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a land acquisition in which the government invoked urgency to dispense with an objections inquiry.
predicates.pre_notification_delay_occurred: A period of delay occurred before the acquisition notification was published.

issues.definition: In an urgent land acquisition proceeding, the fact that delay occurred before publication does not by itself invalidate the government's invocation of urgency.
